title: Fork
text: A fork is one piece attacking two or more enemy pieces at once, so the opponent can only save one. Knights are the classic forking piece because their attacks cannot be blocked; pawn forks and queen forks are also common.

title: Pin
text: A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture. An absolute pin against the king makes moving the pinned piece illegal. Exploit pins by attacking the pinned piece again.

title: Skewer
text: A skewer attacks a valuable piece that must move, exposing a less valuable piece behind it on the same line. It is a reversed pin, delivered by bishops, rooks, and queens.

title: Discovered attack
text: Moving one piece out of the way unmasks an attack by a piece behind it. When the moving piece also creates a threat, the opponent faces two threats in one move. A discovered check is especially forcing.

title: Hanging pieces
text: A hanging piece is undefended and can be captured for free. Before every move, check which of your pieces are attacked and undefended, and whether the opponent left anything en prise.

title: Trade when ahead
text: When you are up material, exchanging pieces simplifies the position and makes the extra material count more. The side that is behind should avoid trades and seek complications.

title: Control the center
text: The central squares d4, d5, e4, e5 let pieces reach both sides of the board quickly. Occupying or controlling the center with pawns and pieces restricts the opponent and supports attacks anywhere.

title: Develop pieces
text: In the opening, bring knights and bishops off the back rank before moving the same piece twice or launching early queen adventures. Every tempo spent developing speeds up castling and central control.

title: King safety and castling
text: Castle early to tuck the king behind pawns and connect the rooks. A king left in the center when the position opens up is vulnerable to checks along open files and diagonals.

title: Open files for rooks
text: Rooks belong on open files, with no pawns, or half-open files, with only enemy pawns. A rook reaching the seventh rank attacks pawns and confines the enemy king.

title: Passed pawns
text: A passed pawn has no enemy pawns in front of it on its file or adjacent files. Passed pawns must be pushed, blockaded, or escorted; in endgames they often decide the game.

title: Back-rank mate
text: When a king is trapped on its back rank by its own pawns, a rook or queen check on that rank can be mate. Creating luft by pushing a pawn next to the king prevents it.

title: Checks, captures, threats
text: A practical calculation order: first look at all checks, then all captures, then moves that create threats. Forcing moves limit the opponent's replies and are where most tactics hide.

title: Doubled and isolated pawns
text: Doubled pawns sit on the same file and isolated pawns have no friendly pawns on adjacent files. Both are structural weaknesses that can become targets, though they can also open files for rooks.

title: Bishop pair
text: Two bishops together cover squares of both colors and are strong in open positions. Giving up the bishop pair is often worth it only for a concrete gain such as damaging the pawn structure.

title: Outposts
text: An outpost is a square that enemy pawns can no longer attack, often in enemy territory. A knight on a supported outpost can be as strong as a rook.

title: King activity in endgames
text: Once queens are off, the king becomes a fighting piece. Centralize it to support pawns and attack enemy pawns; in pawn endgames, opposition often decides the result.

title: Promotion
text: A pawn reaching the last rank promotes, usually to a queen. Races between passed pawns come down to counting moves; check whether the promotion square is controlled and whether the new queen can be captured.

title: Checkmate patterns
text: Recognize common mating nets: back-rank mate, smothered mate with a knight, queen and king mates, and ladder mates with two heavy pieces. Look for checks that remove the king's escape squares.

title: Prophylaxis
text: Prophylaxis means asking what the opponent wants to do and preventing it before improving your own position. Quiet moves that stop a threat are often stronger than an aggressive plan.

title: Space advantage
text: Pawns advanced into the opponent's half gain space, giving your pieces more room and cramping theirs. The cramped side should seek exchanges and pawn breaks to free their game.

title: Pawn breaks
text: A pawn break is a pawn move that challenges the opponent's pawn chain to open lines. Timing breaks when your pieces are ready to use the opened files and diagonals is a core middlegame skill.

title: Material values
text: Rough piece values are pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. Use them to judge trades, but activity, king safety, and structure can outweigh a point of material.

title: Desperado
text: When a piece is going to be lost anyway, it can capture something first to recoup material. Always check whether an attacked piece has a useful capture before retreating it.

title: Removing the defender
text: If a key square or piece is protected by one defender, capture or deflect that defender first. Then the original target falls.
